REVIEW Capitalism, Freedom, and Overdeveloped Nations Capitalism and Freedom. By Milton Friedman. University of Chicago Press, 1962; reprinted in paperback, 1982. 202 pp. $7.95. The Overdeveloped Nations: The Diseconomies of Scale. By Leopold Kohr. Out of print. Raymond Benton, Jr. In 1962 Milton Friedman published Capitalism and Freedom, the same year that Leopold Kohr first pub- lished The Overdeveloped Nations. These two books are parallel in many respects, beginning with their equally negative reactions to President Kennedy's statement in his inaugural address: "Ask not what your country can do for you- ask what you can do for your coun- try. " Both are short, both regard the value of figures to be in their ability to illustrate a philosophic proposition. Neither book when re- issued after about twenty years was updated nor took account of subse- quent work. "If a proposition has validity, " Kohr wrote and Fried- man would agree, "it can be illus- trated by an old set of figures just as well as by a new one." Initially both books were of limited influence. Friedman admits as much in the new preface to the 1982 reissue. We can presume Kohr's book was of limited influ- ence, in the English-speaking world at least. It was first published in German (1962) and translated into Spanish (1965) before being translated into English (1978). In time, however, Friedman's book has not been without influence, much of it due to the influence of Milton Friedman himself. Kohr's influence is less direct than Fried- man's, although it is not less sig- nificant. Peter Gillingham writes that "Leopold Kohr was the man who helped [E. F.] Schumacher clarify his understanding of scale and the tendency of ever-larger sys- tems to create ever-larger prob- RAYMOND BENTON, JR. is Associate Professor of Marketing at the School of Business Administration, Loyola University of Chicago. lems" ("The Making of Good Work, " in Good Work by E. F. Schumacher, Harper Colophon Books, 1979). Both books express much con- cern about the fate of people, their freedom, and about the fate of eco- nomic systems not governed from the center. The books differ in their diagnoses, their prognoses, and in their prescriptions. Friedman argues that what he terms variously the free, private- enterprise exchange economy or competitive capitalism is the best system yet devised by man to guar- antee individual liberty. What is needed, as he sees it, is a recommit- ment in faith to that system. Kohr, on the other hand, while he may well agree with Friedman on the virtues of free enterprise, insists that "A living, dynamic, competi- tive system such as capitalism can . . . function effectively only as long as its units are both numerous and small" (p. 170, f.n.1). Capitalism and freedom Friedman's main intent is to es- tablish "a general presumption against the state. " He does this by pointing out that government inter- vention is improper, dangerous, and generally fails to accomplish what it was intended to do anyway. What disturbs Friedman is the "collectivist trend of the century, " manifest by the increasing inter- vention of government in economic affairs-directly through legisla- tive and administrative acts and in- directly as a buyer of much of our output. In fact, government is the sole buyer of the output of many firms and industries. Friedman's concept of individ- ual freedom is the general absence of political coercion. He does not believe that politics and economics are naturally separate and uncon- nected. He argues that any such November-December 19861Challenge 59 Downloaded by [University of Pennsylvania] at 10:12 10 May 2016

separation is a social creation and that the only system yet devised to separate economic power from po- litical power, thereby protecting in- dividual freedom, is competitive capitalism. But here is the crux of the prob- lem. If economic power is to be separated from political power, then those who are "playing the game" must not have a hand in de- termining the rules by which the game is played. Otherwise, eco- nomic activity is not separated from political authority nor politi- cal activity from economic authori- ty. If the government interferes in economic activities, the system of checks and balances is upset no more than if economic interests participate in determining the rules and object of the game. Either way the system of checks and balances is disturbed and economic strength does not act as a check to political power, and political strength does not act as a check to economic power. Friedman is well aware of this danger. One of his most quoted re- marks is that in a free economy "there is one and only· one social responsibility of business-to use its resources and engage in activi- ties designed to increase its profits so long as it stays within the rules of the game, which is to say, engages in open and free competition, with- out deception or fraud." But he also makes it clear that "it is the responsibility of the rest of us to establish [the] framework of law" within which the day-to-day activi- ties of business take place. Note, however, that his phrasing elimi- nates business interests from taking part in the setting up of that frame- work. The rest of us do not directly interfere through our government with how business people play the game (accepting that it is played according to the rules) and business people do not interfere with setting up those rules. Thus is economic power effectively separated from 60 Challenge/November-December 1986 political power-the object of a free-enterprise exchange economy. Friedman makes it clear that the invisible hand so often referred to in economic discussions is not the market but that of the law. After his passages about the "social respon- sibility of business," and "the re- sponsibility of the rest of us," he makes it clear that it is the frame- work of law that assures "that an individual in pursuing his own in- terest is, to quote Adam Smith again, 'led by an invisible hand.' " Friedman believes that individ- ual freedom can be preserved and extended, but only if we can per- suade our fellow men that free in- stitutions offer a surer way to achieve our separate ends than the coercive power of the state. He is calling on business people to act in a principled manner, but to do so they must know the proper rela- tionship between business and gov- ernment in a free society. He notes that the pressure onthe legislature to enact tariffs, fair- trade laws, import quotas, produc- tion quotas, trade union restrictions on employment, occupational li- censure,etc. invariably comes from members of occupational groups or producer groups. He aims to limit the spread of such 'spe- cial-interest-group pressure. In the absence of institutional arrange- ments to offset that pressure, "pro- ducer groups will invariably have a much stronger influence upon leg- islative action and the powers that be than will the diverse, widely spread [public] interests." Disci- pline and principled action, Fried- man believes, offers the only hope of limiting the spread of special in- terests and continued government intervention in the economy .. As Lewis Mumford wrote in The Story oj Utopias [1922], "The man who 'wholly respects the rights of property is kept out of his neigh- bor's field perhaps even more ef- fectively than the man who is mere- ly forbidden entrance by a no- trespass sign." Or even, we might add, by a wire fence. This is what Friedman means when he states that "underlying most arguments against the free market is a lack of belief in freedom itself." Here he certainly implicates government officials and certain intellectuals, but the comment is addressed to the business community as well. Friedman is concerned with re- versing the collectivist trend of the century, with stemming the influ- ence of government in economic activity by stemming the tide of special-interest-group pressures that are to a large extent responsible for the increasing tide of govern- ment intervention. The overdeveloped nations Leopold Kohr and Milton Fried- man would agree that people do not have to plan chaos and dissolution. That is what happens when the spir- it ceases to be in command. But Kohr's argument is that "a number of the worst economic problems of our time-[including] the seeming- ly irresistible triumph . . . of con- trolled over free-enterprise sys- tems-can be attributed to a single cause: the excessive size of na- tions." Other things are causing difficulties (possibly including a failure of spirit) but they are not primary causal forces because they have been superseded during the last few decades "by a cancerous degree of social overgrowth." Critical social size When problems are caused by pro- portions rather than instititutional orhuman shortcomings, social size has become critical; it has exceeded optimum limits. If a nation were to proclaim a road-safety day, backing it with all the enthusiasm of gov- ernment, police, civic organiza- tions, newspapers, and the clergy, only to discover that the same num- ber of accidents had occurred by Downloaded by [University of Pennsylvania] at 10:12 10 May 2016

noon that had been registered on the corresponding date a year earli- er by nightfall, one might conclude that all the warnings and pleadings against reckless driving had fallen on deaf ears. Kohr uses this exam- ple (the case was Puerto Rico) to demonstrate his principle: "Once a car-driving society has reached critical size, traffic accidents are no longer the resul t of recklessness but of the size of society. " Road-safety days and appeals to reason will not appreciably reduce the accident rate. What is needed is to reduce the effective size of the car-driving so- ciety to sub-critical size, back to within optimum limits. That can be done by reducing the actual number of automobiles, by decreasing their density (perhaps by increasing the width of the roads), or by decreas- ing the speed at which they move about. Only then are accidents the result of personal factors, and only then can they be averted by caution or appeals to reason. "In the case of economic sys- tems [ critical size] sets in when so- cial overgrowth begins to curtail the choice between alternatives, leaving only socialism viable, and even this only for a little while longer. " Choice of an economic system depends on taste and tem- perament, but to have any meaning choice must be exercisable. It is never a matter only of what we want but also of what alternatives are open to us-what we can have. If a community is too small, the ques- tion of socialism versus capitalism becomes irrelevant because compe- tition is replaced by cooperation, property is largely held in com- mon, and work is allocated on the basis of social need rather than per- sonal desire. The purpose of all would be the purpose of each and diversity is eliminated. As too small a community pre- cludes freedom of choice, so does a community that has become too large. Even in the absence of a con- scious socialist movement, social- ization will set in at a given devel- opment stage quite spontaneously. With the purely quantitative growth of problems resulting from increasing numbers, the capitalis- tic, self-balancing mechanisms that operate so satisfactorily at lesser population densities become rigid. This can be dealt with only through an outside controlling agent such as the government. One manifestation ofthis social- ization process in productive ac- tivities is that associated with na- tional defense. When the physical size of the political community has grown beyond a certain size, an un- avoidable militarization sets in as the political leaders find them- selves bordering on other political organisms of such magnitude that they require a disproportionately greater share of social prepared- ness than was necessary as long as states were relatively small. As an increasing fraction of total resources comes to be devoted to defense, the nature of the society changes; something that Friedman clearly recognizes when he writes, "The importance of government as a buyer of so much of our output, and the sole buyer of the output of many firms and industries, ... concentrates a dangerous amount of economic power in the hands of the political authorities, changes the environment in which business operates and the criteria relevant for business success, and in these and other ways endangers a free market." Beyond the question of the mili- tarization of society, overgrown so- cieties have inflated and multiplied the normal problems of life to such dimensions that their solutions eventually outgrow the possibilities of private action. This creates the need for ever-increasing public control and power in other spheres of life. As enterprises become few- er and bigger, a precarious equilib- rium results that is no longer of the same self-regulatory nature that characterized previous periods when enterprises were more nu- merous and smaller. With the loss of an automatically functioning in- ternal balance, a regulatory force must be introduced from outside. Since only society as a whole can furnish such a force, its principal agent, the government, is recalled to the scene and charged to assume, in addition to its political role, also a significant economic role. But if it is to be effective in the face of the giant concerns it faces, its powers must also be increased to such an extent that none of the economic colossi surviving the competitive struggle can challenge its deci- sions. Hence President Franklin D. Roosevelt's comment: "The liber- ty of a democracy is not safe if the people tolerate the growth of pri- vate power to a point where it be- comes stronger than their demo- cratic state itself." It is clear that Kohr attributes to government a role that Friedman does not. Namely, as economic his- torian Karl Polany expressed it in The Great Transformation (1944), that of "altering the rate of change, speeding it up or slowing it down as the case may be" to attain a more or less stable situation so that the difference between the rate of change and the rate of social adjust- ment is not so great that it threatens the social fabric itself. This is not a role for government that Friedman admits because he assumes those stable conditions from the outset: "When we support a free price sys- tem at home," Friedman states, "this does not imply that we favor a system in which prices fluctuate wildly up and down. What we want is a system in which prices are free to fluctuate but in which the forces determining them are sufficiently stable so that in fact prices move within moderate ranges." Too much discretionary power in the hands of government authorities would certainly threaten this kind November-December 19861Challenge 61 Downloaded by [University of Pennsylvania] at 10:12 10 May 2016

of "hoped for" stability. But even that would not be disastrous if it were not for the amplifying effect of the size of the institutions through which whatever price fluc- tuations exist are reverberated. Size cycles Before the industrial revolution the most widely recognized cycles were those of the agricultural sea- sons. The industrial revolution di- minished the significance of farm cycles by replacing them with busi- ness cycles. Business cycles are in- herent in the business system itself. However, as long as the market areas and business units were rela- tively small, the scale of fluctu- ations they could produce were so limited that no external stabilizer was required. As trading areas and business units got bigger, competitive colli- sions and cyclical fluctuations grew in intensity. Increasing size began to assume such proportions that the shocks they produced could no longer be absorbed by the self- balancing mechanism of capital- ism. Who, except the government, could marshal the force necessary to propel an overgrown economy out of the pit of depression once it had landed in it? But -and this is Kohr's central point....,...the element needing government control is not a business cycle but a size cycle. Cyclical fluctuations as such are no more harmful to the economy than breathing is to people. What turns cyclical fluctuations into a problem is the disruptive scale they are able to assume as the economies engendering them outgrow certain proportions. Scale is as external to the economy as are sunspots, "tak- ing its measure not from the system producing cycles but from the size of the society through which the cy- cle is able to transmit itself." As long as theory keeps on mix- ing externally caused size cycles with internally caused business cy- 62 Challenge/November-December 1986 cles, it cannot cope with the prob- lem of business cycles except through the partial or total aboli- tion of the business system. But once it is realized that the true problem is not the business cycle but the size cycle, the damaging in- truder can be eliminated without at the same time eliminating the sys- tem it has invaded. The introduc- tion of social controls is not what is needed. What is needed is a reduc- tion of social size to harmless pro- portions by making the market area through which they can transmit themselves too small to permit dan- gerous amplification. Smaller is better From Leopold Kohr's perspective the increasingly unmanageable complexities in the modern world have their origin not in the nature of the economic system nor in its sup- porting ideology, but in its size. The difficult questions involve de- termining optimum size, and how overgrown societies can be re- turned to optimum properties. The answers will go undiscovered as long as the dominant theme contin- ues to be grow, expand, multiply, increase, speed up, and integrate. There should be no mistake about the significance of such a perspective. Economic growth is still a secular religion in America- a very important creed. It is a source of personal motivation, the basis for political unity, and the one social goal that enjoys unifying commitment. Not to grow, not to expand, to divide rather than multi- ply, to decrease or slow down is as un-American as is socialism. Kohr's size theory strikes at the heart of the cherished belief in the virtue of continued economic growth and expansion. Indeed, he argues, growth in consumption lev- els as well as in other things can be deleterious and could just as well be a sign of worsening as of improving conditions. This brings us to a distinction implied in Kohr's book and not made at all in Friedman's: the dis- tinction between capitalism and free enterprise. In a review of R. Joseph Monsen and Kenneth D. Walter's Nationalized Companies: A Threat to American Business (McGraw-Hill, 1983) published in the New York Review of Books (De- cember 8, 1983, pp. 23-25), Rob- ert Heilbroner wrote that capital- ism can be conceived either as "a system of independent enterprises coordinating its actions through a relatively free market network" or as a system in which the core em- phasis is in "the all-pervasive prin- ciple of the expansion of capital." If the never-satisfied expansion of enterprise is what sets in motion the processes by which capitalism achieves its essential operating suc- cess, establishes its particular form of hierarchy, and pursues its long- term goals, then what is that system which is, at its core, a system of independent enterprises coordinat- ing their actions through a free market network? Free enterprise. Could it be that free enterprise and capitalism, rather than being the same thing, have merely been compatible and that now they are no longer? Could it be that we can have one or the other but not both, at least not as we have known them? Friedman is aware that much has gone on in the "real world" in which people live, but he refuses to admit new evidence, and to address the changes, and is consequently destined to be a greatly disappoint- ed man. His error is his insistence that what is important in this matter of size is relative size rather than absolute size. "The most important fact about enterprise monopoly," he wrote, "is its relative unimpor- tance from the point of view of the economy as a whole. . . . One rea- son for this [mistaken impression that it is important] is the tendency to confuse absolute and relative Downloaded by [University of Pennsylvania] at 10:12 10 May 2016

size. As the economy has grown, enterprises have become larger in absolute size. This has been taken to mean that they account for a larg- er fraction of the market, whereas the market may have grown even faster. " This type of reasoning sug- gests that while it is true that enter- prises have gotten absolutely larg- er, they may also have gotten relatively smaller. At any rate, when Friedman states that "our minds tell us, and history confirms, that the great threat to freedom is the concentration of power . . . whether in governmental or private hands," the reader is expected to believe that a small-town grocery store that has 75 percent ofthe local market is a greater threat to free- dom than the transnational mega- enterprise commanding resources and generating revenues exceeding those of most nation states, because that firm has only a 25 percent share of the global market. To this, Kohr would object that if the issue of freedom is about interpersonal relations, as Friedman states, then size matters-and it matters abso- lutely, for Man is the measure of all things, not the market. Friedman also displayed a pen- chant for hiding the incontrovert- ible fact that the cumulative effect of changes in our economic institu- tions over the last century has in- deed created a fundamentally dif- ferent type of economic system. Friedman does this through his choice of metaphors, by depicting large economic institutions as just another manifestation of markets where people come together to sell their labor and to buy goods. He asks that the large, complex mod- ern economy be looked at as if it were a 17th century agricultural economy of self-sufficient house- holds, and addresses and exempli- fies his' 'principles" by drawing on "the most competitive sectors of the economy." It is not these sec- tors that are responsible for the col- lectivist trend of the century. He should not so steadfastly refrain from applying his principles to the least competitive sectors of the economy, rather than concentrating on those in which the institutions and the size of markets are within ranges that fit his model. Because we have no institutional safeguards to prevent the concen- tration of power, whether in public or private hands, Friedman should encourage as a proper economic motive not the making of as much money as possible but only as much as necessary. We should replace "more is better," with "enough is best. " Friedman believed that we would be able to preserve and ex- tend freedom despite the size of the military programs and despite the economic powers already concen- trated in Washington (dangers, he states, "we cannot avoid") by per- suading others "that free institu- tions offer a surer, if perhaps at times a slower, route to the ends LETTERS they seek than the coercive power of the state. " To this Leopold Kohr responds that' 'the only way to pro- tect the members of an overgrown community from the implications of a life in common and its rationa- lization in the form of a collectivist philosophy is not the preaching of an anti-collectivist philosophy but the destruction of the condition of which collectivism is nothing but a natural concomitant -excessive so- cial size." Capitalism and Freedom and The Overdeveloped Nations are companion volumes. They should be read together because by so do- ing we may discover why, when the current experiments in Washington are over, we failed to curb the col- lectivist trend of the century. We will know, or at least seriously sus- pect, that it is because we gave up everything but the cause of our own undoing. Capitalism, freedom, and overdevelopment: we are, perhaps yet, free to choose. The editor cordially invites readers to send letters to Challenge, 80 Business Park Drive, Armonk, N. Y. 10504. The Real Deficit Professor Wonnacott makes a most curious objection to inflation-ad- justing the deficit, as proposed by Robert Eisner and endorsed in my review of his book (Challenge, September/October, 1986). He seems to be saying that because a little knowledge is a dangerous thing, we ought to make do with less knowledge. It would be more inspiring to hope that improve- ments in accounting would lead us away from, and not toward, rigid policy rules not supported by eco- nomic thought. In particular, measuring the real deficit accurately in no way leads to the general "rule" that the real budget should be balanced. Who- ever suggested such a rule?
